summary: This benchmark evaluates cross-model activation patching between Qwen2.5-Coder-7B (donor) and Qwen2.5-14B (host) across 512 two-operand Python arithmetic groups under open-vocabulary generation. The study demonstrates 100% success (512/512) for translated donor activation edits and full host state replacements, contrasted against 0/512 for norm-matched random controls. The benchmarking methodology is rigorous with thorough negative and positive controls, though the domain remains restricted to single-token, single-step arithmetic.
strengths: Rigorous experimental controls, featuring both norm-matched orthogonal random edits (0/512 passed) as a negative control and full host state exchange (512/512 passed) as an upper bound ceiling.
Elimination of shortlist constraints by validating top-1 rank across the entire 152,064-token vocabulary rather than relying on artificial 4-choice classification.
Precise reproducibility specification, including exact commit revisions for both Qwen2.5 models and exact versions for the Python/MLX stack.
Clear separation and balanced representation across arithmetic operations (256 addition groups and 256 subtraction groups with 4 variants each).
weaknesses: Narrow benchmark scope confined to single-digit, single-step arithmetic expressions within structured Python variable assignment statements.
Omission of specific hardware details (e.g., exact Mac Studio SoC configuration such as M2 Ultra or M3 Max) despite reporting runtime down to the second.
The 7x7 linear projection map derivation and training/calibration protocol are not self-contained in the text and rely on external links.
suggestions: Expand evaluation to multi-digit arithmetic and multi-token generation to test whether linear representation transfer degrades when crossing token boundaries.
Document the exact Apple Silicon SoC specifications and unified memory capacity alongside execution time.
Provide a brief mathematical formulation of the 7x7 linear map fitting procedure directly in the methodology section.

claims.text: The Studio run took three minutes and 21 seconds using Python 3.12, MLX 0.32.4, MLX-LM 0.32.2 and NumPy 2.5.5.
